This paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation, which is a fundamental task in computer vision. Our method leverages the power of constraint propagation to efficiently segment images into their constituent parts. We introduce a fast and effective algorithm that leverages the spatial and semantic relationships between pixels to propagate constraints and accurately separate objects from the background.

Existing methods for image segmentation often rely on computationally expensive techniques such as iterative optimization or deep learning, which can be limiting for real-time applications. In contrast, our approach is designed to be fast and efficient, making it suitable for real-time deployment.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several benchmark datasets, showing that it produces high-quality segmentation masks with accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art methods while being significantly faster. Our experiments also reveal that our approach is robust to various challenges such as noise, occlusions, and cluttered scenes.

The key contribution of this paper is the development of a fast and efficient algorithm for image segmentation using constraint propagation. Our approach has important implications for a wide range of applications, including object detection, tracking, and scene understanding. It has the potential to significantly improve the performance of various computer vision systems, including autonomous vehicles, surveillance systems, and medical imaging devices.

In summary, this paper presents a fast and efficient method for image segmentation using constraint propagation, which has important implications for real-time computer vision applications. Our approach is robust, accurate, and efficient, making it a valuable contribution to the field of computer vision.

This paper proposes a novel approach for measuring the thickness of head overcoats using a deep learning model called NASNet-Large-Decoder Net. The proposed method utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) to estimate the thickness of head overcoats from images, without the need for manual measurement or invasive techniques.

The NASNet-Large-Decoder Net model is trained on a large dataset of images of heads with varying overcoat thicknesses, and is designed to accurately detect the thickness of the overcoat based on features extracted from the images. The model is evaluated on a test set of images and shows high accuracy and robustness in measuring overcoat thickness, outperforming traditional methods that rely on manual measurement or simple image processing techniques.

The proposed method has important implications for the textile industry, as it provides a fast, accurate, and non-invasive way to measure the thickness of head overcoats, which is a key factor in determining the quality and warmth of the garment. The use of deep learning techniques also allows for real-time measurement, enabling manufacturers to quickly and accurately assess the quality of their products.

Overall, this paper demonstrates the potential of deep learning techniques for improving the measurement of head overcoat thickness, and highlights the advantages of using NASNet-Large-Decoder Net for this task. The proposed method has the potential to revolutionize the textile industry by providing a more efficient and accurate way to measure the thickness of head overcoats, leading to improved product quality and customer satisfaction.

This paper proposes a new method of measuring the thickness of a hat using a deep learning method, NASNet-Large-Decoder-Net. This method is based on a convolutional neural network (CNN) that is used to estimate the thickness of the hat from the image, without the need for manual measurement and a way of destroying it. This NASNet-Large-Decoder-Net is trained by a large number of images of the heads of people of different hat thicknesses, and by extracting the key features of the images, we can accurately predict the thickness of the hat. The performance of the proposed method has been evaluated using images of different thicknesses of hats, and the proposed method outperforms the existing manual measurement and simple image processing methods. The proposed method has a significant impact on the textile industry because it provides a quick, accurate, non-destructive and a means of determining the quality and warmth of the garment. At the same time, it is a real-time measurement that can quickly and accurately determine the quality of the manufacturer's product. This paper demonstrates the potential of deep learning to improve the thickness measurement of the hat, and it shows the advantages of NASNet-Large-Decoder-Net for this task. The proposed method has the potential to transform the textile industry, with the aim of obtaining more efficient and accurate measurements of the thickness of the hat, which will lead to the improvement of the quality of the product and the satisfaction of consumers.

This paper proposes a new deep learning approach to image segmentation, combining the advantages of region, edge, and contour models. Specifically, it integrates the existing region, edge, and contour models into a single neural network. The region model can induce the features learned to have the characteristics of homogeneous regions, and the edge and contour models can enhance the features to have the characteristics of edges and contours. We have performed experiments on several public data sets, including semantic segmentation, object detection, and image-to-image matching, and the results are superior to existing methods in accuracy, efficiency, and robustness. We also perform a partial ablation analysis on the components of the model, and prove that the integration of three models can achieve better performance than the individual use of each model. This paper makes the following contributions: [1] It proposes a deep learning architecture combining the advantages of region, edge, and contour models in automatic image segmentation; [2] the integration of region, edge, and contour into a single neural network; [3] superior performance in various image segmentation tasks; [4] a thorough analysis and verification of the proposed method using partial ablation experiments; [5] The proposed method is of wide application value, and can be used in a wide range of applications, such as self-driving, medical imaging, robots, and artificial vision. We can achieve accurate and efficient image segmentation, which in turn enables the performance of the downstream task of object recognition, scene understanding, and reasoning.

Dynamic adaptive mixture models (DAMMs) are an innovative statistical approach that allows for flexible clustering and classification of data in an evolving environment. DAMMs use a dynamic process to update model parameters as new data becomes available, resulting in improved accuracy and adaptability. This paper provides an overview of DAMMs, including their theoretical foundations and practical implementation. We also discuss applications of DAMMs in various fields and highlight their advantages over traditional clustering and classification techniques. Overall, DAMMs offer a powerful and versatile tool for analyzing complex datasets in dynamic settings, and their potential impact on the field of statistics and data analysis is significant.

Dynamic Adaptive Mixture Models (DAMMs) are an effective way to cluster and classify data in changing environments. The DAMMs rely on a dynamic process that continually adjusts the model to changing circumstances, resulting in improved accuracy and adaptability. This paper gives an overview of the DAMMs, presenting their theoretical foundations and practical implementations. Various DAMM applications are also discussed, including their advantages over traditional clustering and classification methods. DAMMs are a versatile and powerful tool for complex data analysis in dynamic settings.

This research investigates large-scale image segmentation using structured loss-based deep learning techniques for connectome reconstruction. The study demonstrates how this approach can effectively segment complex images and improve connectivity mapping in brain networks, which has significant implications for neuroscience research and clinical applications. Results show that the proposed method outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency, making it a promising solution for tackle big data challenges in biology imaging analytics. Overall, these findings highlight the potential of advanced machine learning algorithms to revolutionize our understanding of neural circuits underlying cognitive processes and diseases, paving the way towards personalized medicine approaches targeting dysregulated neuronal pathways. Further work is needed to validate the generalizability of the model across different species and tissues types; however,this novel methodology provides compelling evidence supporting its applicability as an essential toolkit within future interconnected omics pipelines addressing complexity science at all levels bioimaging analysis.

It shows that this method can effectively segment complex images and map brain networks to a higher accuracy, which is very important for both scientific research and clinical application. Its high accuracy and speed have a positive effect on the reconstruction of the brain. In addition, the generalizability of this model must be validated in other species and tissues. But this new method shows that it can be used as an important tool in the framework of the omics framework to map out the brain's complexity.

CASSOD-Net is a novel deep learning architecture that utilizes cascaded and separable structures of dilated convolution for embedded vision systems and applications. This architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance while minimizing computational complexity and memory requirements, making it ideal for resource-constrained devices. The use of dilated convolution allows for improved feature extraction and spatial robustness, while the cascaded and separable architecture enables efficient processing. Overall, CASSOD-Net offers a powerful and efficient solution for a wide range of embedded vision tasks.

In this article, we propose a novel neural network architecture based on cascade and separable dilated convolutional layers for embedded vision systems and applications. This architecture is able to provide a good performance while reducing both computation time and memory requirements, making it a good candidate for resource-constrained systems. Dilation convolution allows a better extraction of features, and a better spatial fidelity, while the cascade and separable structure makes it easier to process. As a result, CASSOD-Net provides a strong and efficient neural network for various embedded vision applications.

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDCA) has been used in many applications, such as image segmentation and object detection. However, UDCA requires that the task be explicitly specified by the user. In this work we propose an approach based on task driven generative models (TGM), which allows users to specify their own tasks without having to write any code. We present a novel TGM framework that can automatically generate tasks for arbitrary domains. Our model uses a combination of two different approaches: (i) a supervised learning algorithm that learns a set of latent variables that describe the task; and (ii) a reinforcement learning algorithm that learns a set of actions that are required to complete the task. The resulting task representations are then fed into a generic task generator, which generates tasks for each domain. This approach enables us to use existing machine learning algorithms to learn tasks for arbitrary domains. We demonstrate our method using a variety of datasets including images, videos, and audio files.

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) has been used in many applications, such as image segmentation and object detection. But UDCA needs the task to be expressed in terms of a specific example. In this paper we propose an approach based on a task-driven generative model (T-G), where the task is defined by the network. We present a novel framework that automatically generates tasks for arbitrary domains by combining two approaches. A supervised learning approach that learns latent variables that can express the task, and a reinforcement learning approach that learns the action sequence to complete the task. The resulting task representations are used by a generic task generator, which generates tasks for each domain. This approach makes it possible to learn tasks for any domain with existing machine learning models. We show the effectiveness of our method on images, videos, and sounds.

A Neural Network and its Connectivity to Emotions through Eye Movement (2016) Abstract | PDF


Abstract This study describes an eye movement-based method to generate images based on eye movements rather than eyes themselves, generating both realistic looking faces and fictional characters with emotional features such as fear. To obtain this effect, we first used a convolutional neural network model that trained in three different training cases, each one depending on how well it could reconstruct high quality real facial data from videos or eye images. We then applied these models to simulate face detection tasks using real videos and an initial database of 300 movies representing 40 genres, including action, horror movies (e.g., "Paranormal Activity"), thrillers (i.e., such as the films of Quentin Tarantino), sci-fi, horror, science fiction, fantasy, and horror films, plus other short subjects like commercials, TV shows and popular songs [1]. The results showed our software could successfully recognize the faces accurately even when it was trained only once and was not updated to learn specific scenes from real events, although the ability to create new movies remained unclear. Next we aimed to improve the accuracy by finding more robust neural networks based on natural language processing [2], which can be learned more efficiently compared to ConvNets. However, again very few papers have been published about that subject; however, previous work from our group showed that two deep learning frameworks are sufficient but it remains up to future work to prove the effectiveness of recurrent networks based on LSTM networks in predicting eye behaviors [3]. In particular, another recent report has demonstrated the efficiency of a recurrent neural network, combined with LSTM layers that could provide better results on certain types of emotions. It seems possible to build higher performance recurrent network via stochastic gradient descent over a layer of backpropagation where parameters have weights dependent on data. Since the application required no special knowledge from the user, it might increase the availability of computer vision applications at all skill levels.

> We consider jet-like solutions to the Euler equations, which are characterized by an exponential decay in one direction and polynomial growth in another. These solutions have been used as building blocks for constructing global weak solutions to the compressible Navier–Stokes equations with vacuum [1]. In this work we study the linearized version of these jets, namely the solution to the homogeneous Euler equation that decays exponentially fast along the $z$-axis and grows polynomially in the transverse directions $(x,y)$. This problem can be viewed as a generalization of the classical Riemann problem, where the initial data has compact support on the plane but does not vanish at infinity. Our main result shows that there exists a unique solution to this problem, provided that the initial data satisfies certain compatibility conditions. Moreover, we show that the solution depends continuously on the initial data in the Sobolev space $\dot{H}^s(\mathbb{R}^{2+1})$ for any $s\geq 0$.

We consider jet-like solutions to the Euler equations, characterized by exponential decay in one direction and polynomial growth in the other. These solutions have been used as a basis for the construction of global weak solutions to the compressible Navier–Stokes equations in the incompressible case. In the present paper, we consider the linearized version of these jets, that is the solution to the homogeneous Euler equation which decays rapidly along the z-axis and grows polynomially in the (x,y) transverse directions. The problem under study can be regarded as a generalization of the Riemann–Hilbert problem, with the additional feature that the initial data is bounded on the plane but does not vanish at infinity. Our main result is that there is a unique solution to this problem, subject to some initial data conditions. Moreover, we show that the solution depends continuously on the initial data in the Sobolev space H_s(R2+).

> Crowdsourcing has recently become essential to solve important real tasks, including annotation for Computer Vision (CV). It can offer solutions at low cost and in large scales; however, it often produces noise as well. In this work, we study how online click streams generated by crowdsources or users could be used efficiently and effectively for filtering the collected noisy crowd based image regions to improve various down stream applications such as localization or classification which rely on object detection with high accuracy. We demonstrate that the information provided within the click streams contain very meaningful clues about what the user/crowdsource are trying to highlight with respect to object categories they want to segment offline. Our proposed algorithm makes use first of statistical information over multiple online click paths that form a sequence. This is followed by a dynamic programming method able to maximize object recognition performance in terms of precision and recall using these estimated statistics. To the best our knowledge this is among the first methods to extract object boundaries directly from raw online behaviors without relying on any ground truth labels or supervision signal. Since click paths naturally reflect human vision, we show its power by comparing with other state of art approaches across different datasets demonstrating significant improvements

Moreover, the method of crowd-sourced annotating has recently become an important tool for addressing practical problems, especially annotation for Computer Vision. Crowd-based annotation can provide solutions for large-scale, low-cost tasks, but often it also produces some noise. In this paper, we study how to filter the collected noisy crowd-based image regions to improve applications that rely on accurate object detection, such as object localization and classification. We prove that the information contained in the crowd-based clicks can provide very useful hints about the categories that the crowd source is interested in and wants to highlight in the image. Our approach uses the statistical information of a sequence of online clicks. We use the statistics obtained to optimize the object recognition performance in terms of precision and recall. To our knowledge, this is one of the first methods to extract object boundaries directly from raw crowd-based behaviour without any ground truth labels or supervision signals. Since the clicks of a crowd source resemble human visual features, we show its power by comparing with other methods on different data sets and obtaining significant improvements.

> We propose to use progressively diffused networks (PDN) as an alternative approach to semantic image segmentation, which can be trained end-to-end in an efficient manner and achieve state-of-the-art performance on several benchmarks. Our method consists of two main components: 1) A coarse-to-fine network architecture that gradually increases the resolution of feature maps during training; 2) An iterative refinement process that uses a diffusion mechanism to propagate information between adjacent layers. In contrast with previous methods based on fully convolutional neural networks or recurrent architectures, our PDN model does not require any postprocessing steps such as CRF or graph cuts. Experiments show that our method achieves competitive results compared to other approaches while being significantly faster at test time.

OUR METHOD WE propose a method of semantic image recognition that is quite simple in its train-ing, and which achieves a very good result in its accuracy on several of the standard images. Our method consists of two parts: a progressively finer neural network which gradually increases the resolution of its feature maps as it proceeds; a diffusion process which propagates between layers information derived by the preceding layer. Unlike methods based on convolutional or recurrent neural networks, our PDN model does not require any post-processing steps such as Connected Region Growing or graph cutting. Experiments show that our method produces results which are very satisfactory compared with other methods, and that its recognition time is much less than that of these methods.

This academic paper presents a novel partially reversible U-Net architecture for volumetric image segmentation. Our method is designed to increase memory efficiency while maintaining high performance. We achieve this by incorporating a novel dynamic memory allocation scheme that allows for a partial reversal of the segmentation process. This scheme reduces the memory footprint by eliminating the need for storing additional intermediate results during prediction. We evaluate our method on various volumetric medical imaging datasets and show that it achieves state-of-the-art results with less memory usage than previous approaches.

This article presents a new architecture of a partially reversible U-Net, used to segment volumetric images. Our method is intended to increase the memory efficiency of the U-Net, while maintaining a high performance, and it is achieved by a dynamic allocation of memory that allows for a partial reversal of the process. This reduces the memory requirements, because it avoids the need to store intermediate results during the learning process. We tested our method on various medical image data sets and showed that it can achieve state-of-the-art results with less memory than previous methods.

The search of effective neural architectures is an essential task in deep learning applications. Recent advances have shown promising results in Automatic Neural Network Design (A-NNAD), but still face many challenges when it comes to image segmentation, where complex and hierarchical patterns exist. In this context, a new architecture has been proposed called Deep Convolutional Neural Architecture Search by Network Anchors with Sampling techniques (DCNAS). DCNAS is based on densely connected layers that replace traditional sequential structures, allowing to explore more complex and diverse network topologies efficiently. This approach aims at improving the current limitations, addressing connectivity constraints and maximizing the exploration space while leveraging prior knowledge from anchor networks.

The experimental evaluation exhibits significant improvements over the state-of-the-art methods in several benchmarks. For instance, our approach achieves competitive performances with less time and computational resources than other approaches while keeping its model size relatively constant. Furthermore, we also perform ablation studies highlighting the importance of specific components such as sampling techniques or density distributions on the performance of our obtained models, which reveals insights into the design criteria. Our proposed method opens up new possibilities in A-NNAD applied to semantic image segmentation, paving the way towards efficient and high-performance automatic neural architecture discovery.

The search for an effective neural network is an essential task in deep learning applications. Recent advances have shown promise in the field of automatic neural network design (ANNAD), but are still facing many problems in image segmentation where there are complex and hierarchical patterns. In this context, a new neural network has been developed, which is called Deep Convolutional Neural Architecture Search by Sampling with Node-level Resets (DCNAS). Using highly interconnected layers in place of the traditional sequential layers makes it possible to efficiently explore complex and diverse network topologies. The aim is to overcome the limitations of previous methods by reducing the constraints on connectivity and by exploring as many possible connections as possible while using prior knowledge from anchor networks. The experiments show considerable improvements over existing methods on a series of experiments. For example, our approach obtains a higher performance in a shorter time, with less memory and a lower power consumption, while the size of the network remains relatively stable. We also conducted experiments on the effects of specific elements such as the sampling technique and the distribution of nodes on the performance of the obtained networks, which gives insights into the design criteria. Our proposed method opens up new possibilities in ANNAD applied to semantic image segmentation and paves the way for efficient and high-performance ANNAD.

The Lovász-Softmax loss is a novel optimization technique for neural networks that aims to improve the intersection-over-union (IoU) measure, which is a commonly used metric for object detection and segmentation tasks. The IoU measure measures the overlap between two objects and is a key component of many deep learning models. However, optimizing the IoU measure directly can be challenging due to its non-differentiable nature. The Lovász-Softmax loss addresses this issue by providing a tractable surrogate for the IoU measure that can be optimized using gradient descent. The Lovász-Softmax loss is based on the Lovász-Hadamard theorem, which relates the IoU measure to the Lovász-Softmax function. The Lovász-Softmax function is a generalization of the softmax function that can be used to model complex probability distributions. The Lovász-Softmax loss is shown to outperform other optimization techniques for the IoU measure, including the cross-entropy loss and the focal loss. The paper also provides experimental results that demonstrate the effectiveness of the Lovász-Softmax loss in object detection and segmentation tasks. Overall, the Lovász-Softmax loss provides a powerful optimization technique for neural networks that can improve the performance of deep learning models in a wide range of applications.

The IoU measure is difficult to optimize directly, due to its non-differentiable character. Loss-Softmax solves this problem by introducing a differentiable, IoU-based surrogate that can be approximated by gradient descent. In this paper, we propose a spatio-temporal data-driven pooling (STD2P) method for semantic segmentation from an RGB-D video. The STD2P method first segments an RGB-D video into several time intervals according to their appearance and dynamic characteristics. For each time interval, we then estimate its semantic label by using a spatio-temporal data-driven pooling method. The semantic label decision for each time interval is made by aggregating the local spatial-temporal information within the interval using a superpixel-based method. Finally, the semantic labels of all the time intervals are integrated to produce the final segmentation result of the video. The STD2P method is designed to effectively utilize the spatio-temporal information in an RGB-D video for semantic segmentation. Experimental results on two publicly available datasets, namely the NYU Depth V2 dataset and the LineMod dataset, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

We then sum up the semantic labels for all of the sections to give the final result for the whole sequence. We call this method STD2P, which makes effective use of the spatio-temporal information of an RGB-D sequence for semantic segmentation. We propose a method to identify linear regressions with heteroskedastic errors in all variables, including the independent ones. Recent progress in deep learning has achieved great performance in biomedical image segmentation, especially with the popularization of U-Net and its variants. In this paper, we tackle the image segmentation problem where pre-segmentation of the foreground is available, i.e., images are annotated with imperfect bounding boxes. We propose a Multi-Compound Transformer (MCT) that takes advantage of the available pre-segmentations. Our MCT explicitly models the multiple compounds within each image and dynamically discovers an optimal partition for each input. It leverages the pre-segmentations to model the known structures, while simultaneously learning to discover the unknown structures. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on three public segmentation benchmarks: ISBI 2018 Cardiac MRI Segmentation Challenge, ISBI 2013 Joint Electron Microscopy and Transmission Electron Microscopy Cell Classification, and CASIA BMH2018. Compared with the state-of-the-art methods, our approach achieves promising results.

The ease with which digital information can be preserved, copied, and disseminated online is transforming how we understand collective memory. There are elements of collective memory that until recently were relatively stable, sustained over long periods of time, and subject to limited revision. We begin by identifying four important aspects of collective memory that are changing as a result of the digital revolution: persistence, popularity, authenticity, and hierarchy. Last, we identify four consequences that follow from the digital reshaping of collective memory for the politics of remembering and forgetting.

Multi-focus image fusion is an important technique in image processing that aims to combine multiple images with different focus levels into a single image with enhanced overall focus. The proposed method first calculates the similarity between each pixel in the input images using a similarity measure. Then, a weight map is generated based on the similarity values, which is used to assign weights to each pixel in the input images. Finally, the weighted average of the input images is computed to obtain the fused image. Experimental results on a dataset of multi-focus images demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both visual quality and objective evaluation metrics. The proposed method is also computationally efficient, making it suitable for real-time applications.

The 34-year-old, who won 77 caps for England between 2009 and 2016, made more than 50 appearances in the Premiership during spells at Wasps and Northampton Saints.

He also played for Stade Francais and Ricoh Black Rams in Japan before joining French side Rouen this year.

“I’ve had an amazing career,” said Haskell. “It was always my dream to play professionally.”

A statement on Haskell’s website added that he will now focus on other business interests including property development and media work.

### ‘Proud to have represented England’

Born in Australia but raised in New Zealand, Haskell moved to London as a teenager and joined Wasps after playing for Saracens.

His international debut came against Argentina in June 2009 and he went on to win 77 caps – scoring seven tries – until being dropped by Eddie Jones ahead of the 2018 Six Nations Championship.

In total, he scored 10 tries in 11 Tests for the British & Irish Lions, having been selected for their tours of South Africa (2009) and Australia (2013).

“To represent your country is something I am very proud of,” said Haskell. “Playing for England was one of the greatest honours of my life.

“My family are English so it meant everything to me to be able to pull on the red rose jersey and do them proud.

“I would like to thank all those people who helped me along the way; coaches, teammates, friends and family. It wouldn’t have happened without you.”

The rules surrounding sports betting are under intense scrutiny as concerns regarding the integrity and fairness of the industry continue to mount. With an increasing number of betting scandals and match-fixing allegations emerging, experts and lawmakers are calling for stricter regulations to protect the integrity of sports.

In recent years, there have been numerous cases where athletes and individuals involved in sports have been found guilty of manipulating results and betting on their own games. These incidents have raised questions about the effectiveness of current betting laws and whether they are sufficient to deter and penalize individuals involved in such activities.

One key area of concern is the relationship between athletes and betting companies. Many athletes, especially in popular sports such as football or basketball, have sponsorship deals or endorsements with gambling companies. Critics argue that this creates conflicts of interest and can compromise the integrity of the game.

Another issue is the rising popularity of online betting platforms. The accessibility and anonymity provided by these platforms have made it easier for individuals to place bets and potentially engage in fraudulent activities. This has led to calls for more stringent age verification measures and stricter regulations on online gambling.

Lawmakers are also exploring the possibility of implementing a central sports betting oversight body or regulator to ensure the proper enforcement of rules and investigate any suspected wrongdoing. Such a body could collaborate with sports organizations and law enforcement agencies to effectively combat match-fixing and improve the transparency of the industry.

Moreover, there is a growing consensus that education and awareness campaigns are crucial in tackling the root causes of match-fixing. By educating athletes, coaches, and officials about the consequences and risks associated with betting on sports, it is hoped that they will be more conscious of the ethical implications and therefore less likely to engage in fraudulent activities.

While efforts are being made to address these issues, there are challenges that authorities and regulators face. For instance, the global nature of sports and betting makes it difficult to regulate and enforce rules consistently across countries. Additionally, the rapid pace of technological advancements poses new challenges in detecting and investigating illicit activities related to betting.

Nevertheless, it is clear that action needs to be taken to protect the integrity of sports and maintain public trust. Stricter regulations, enhanced oversight, and increased awareness can collectively contribute to a safer and more transparent sports betting industry. Only through such measures can the harms associated with sports betting be mitigated and the reputation of sports upheld.

Ingredients:

* 1 1/2 cups plain frozen yogurt
* 1/2 cup granulated sugar
* 1/4 cup cornstarch
* 1/4 cup unsalted butter, melted
* 2 cups fresh strawberries, hulled and sliced
* 1/2 cup strawberry jam
* 1/2 cup cream cheese, softened
* 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
* 1/4 teaspoon salt
* Whipped cream and additional sliced strawberries for topping (optional)

Instructions:

1. In a medium-sized bowl, whisk together the sugar, cornstarch, and melted butter until well combined.
2. In a separate bowl, mix together the strawberries, strawberry jam, and 1/4 cup of the sugar mixture until the strawberries are well coated.
3. In a large bowl, combine the frozen yogurt, cream cheese, vanilla extract, and salt. Mix until smooth.
4. Fold in the strawberry mixture until well combined.
5. Pour the mixture into an ice cream maker and churn according to the manufacturer's instructions.
6. Once the mixture has finished churning, transfer it to an airtight container and freeze for at least 2 hours.
7. Once the frozen yogurt has frozen, scoop it into bowls and top with whipped cream and additional sliced strawberries, if desired.
8. Serve immediately and enjoy!

Note: If you don't have an ice cream maker, you can also place the mixture in a freezer-safe container and freeze for at least 2 hours, stirring every 30 minutes until the desired consistency is reached.

In fact, here is allrecipes.co.uk's definition of salsa verde:
While there is a lot of variation across the recipes listed, there are still some strong consistencies.
The majority define salsa verde as a sauce made from parsley, garlic, and olive oil. Other herbs that were listed include mint, basil, and oregano. Chives were also mentioned. A handful of recipes mentioned capers in addition to the garlic. The use of nuts in the salsa was a controversial point, with many saying nuts should avoid being added while others insisted they were a mandatory ingredient.
Capers, nuts, and garlic
The above consistency aside, there was very little agreement on the proportions and process. The majority said parsley was a primary ingredient in their recipe, with parsley sometimes listed in the definition of the sauce. However, some recipes left out the parsley altogether. A number of recipes did call for basil; it was most frequently listed alongside the parsley.
Recipes also differed on whether other herbs were added or a primary ingredient. Mint and oregano were the most frequently listed other herbs, though basil was often called for as well.
The recipes listed garlic in every case. However, recipes varied on the amount of garlic. A common amount was "3" or "3 cloves," but there was variation ranging as low as 1 clove and as high as "as much as you like!"
As mentioned before, several recipes did call out the use of nuts, such as walnuts, almonds and pecans.
The amount of oil in the recipe was also varied, though olive oil was listed in every case. The amount of oil ranged from a drizzle of olive oil to a cup of olive oil.
The most consistent aspect of all the recipes, surprisingly, was the mention of vinegar. All of the recipes mentioned something about an element of vinegar. Vinegar that was called to the front in recipes include balsamic vinegar, champagne vinegar, red wine vinegar and white wine vinegar.
As I mentioned, it seemed the general public were split on how to create the best salsa verde. The most frequent response to the question of whether nuts are an appropriate ingredient in a salsa verde was that they should be avoided and that it really is a salsa and not a pesto.

Basically, it is true that there are many recipes on the web, but there are also a lot of constants: in most of the recipes there is a sauce of parsley, garlic and olive oil. The use of nuts in the sauce is controversial: some say that nuts should not be used, others that they are necessary. Title: One Pot Wonder Spanish Paella

Ingredients:
- 2 tablespoons olive oil
- 1 onion, diced

- 1 yellow bell pepper, diced
- 2 tomatoes, diced

Title: Simply Sensational Strawberry Shortcake

Preparation Time: 20 minutes
Cooking Time: 15 minutes
Total Time: 35 minutes
Serves: 8

Ingredients:
- 2 pounds (900g) fresh strawberries, hulled and sliced
- 1/2 cup granulated sugar
- 2 tablespoons lemon juice
- 2 cups all-purpose flour
- 2 tablespoons sugar
- 1 tablespoon baking powder
- 1/2 teaspoon salt
- 1/2 cup unsalted butter, cold and cubed
- 3/4 cup milk
- 2 cups heavy cream
- 1/4 cup powdered sugar
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract

Instructions:

1. In a large bowl, combine sliced strawberries, granulated sugar, and lemon juice. Stir gently until sugar is dissolved, then set aside to allow the flavors to meld while you prepare the shortcake.

2. Preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

3. In a separate bowl, whisk together the all-purpose flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt.

4. Add the cold, cubed butter to the flour mixture. Use a pastry cutter or your fingers to cut the butter into the dry ingredients until the mixture resembles coarse crumbs.

5. Pour in the milk and stir until just combined. Be careful not to overmix - the dough should be slightly sticky.

6. Transfer the dough to a floured surface and knead it gently for a minute until it comes together. Pat the dough into a 1-inch thick rectangle.

7. Using a round cookie cutter or a glass, cut out shortcakes from the dough and place them on the prepared baking sheet.

8. Bake for 12-15 minutes, or until the shortcakes are golden brown. Remove from the oven and allow them to cool completely on a wire rack.

9. Meanwhile, in a chilled bowl, whip the heavy cream, powdered sugar, and vanilla extract until stiff peaks form. Set aside.

10. To assemble the strawberry shortcakes, slice each cooled shortcake in half horizontally.

11. Spoon a generous amount of the strawberry mixture onto the bottom half of the shortcake.

12. Top with a dollop of whipped cream, then place the top half of the shortcake on top.

13. Optional: Add more sliced strawberries and a dusting of powdered sugar on top for extra flavor and presentation.

14. Repeat with the remaining shortcakes

I've been struggling with feelings of guilt lately, and I'm starting to realize that it's because I've been faking things way too much.

I've always been someone who tries to put on a brave face and pretend like everything is fine, even when it's not. I don't know why I do this - maybe it's because I don't want to burden others with my problems or maybe it's because I'm afraid of being vulnerable. The worst part is that I've started to feel like I'm living a lie. I'll put on a happy face and act like everything is great, even though inside I'm feeling overwhelmed and lost. It's like I'm living in a constant state of denial, and it's taking a toll on my mental health.

Here is what I do when I catch myself overthinking things before saying them – which tends to happen a lot since I’m pretty introverted.

I try to focus on listening more carefully to what the other person is saying, while at the same time trying to formulate a response in my head. Then I consider: would I say this in real life without overthinking it? If the answer is yes, then I say it.

This takes practice, and doesn’t always work, but I find that it helps capture the spontaneity that often gets lost when I overthink things.

Michael awakens the next morning, having slept through a whole season of Desperately Seeking Susan—and he decides to take advantage of “Instant Replay”—in between sleep cycles, as it turns out.

The verdict is starkly divided among viewers, some of whom feel the film falls short compared to other Marvel entries, while others appreciate its standalone charm, without the imperative need to be entwined in the larger universe.

Edward Norton's portrayal of Bruce Banner is nuanced and engaging. He captures the internal conflict of his character superbly, giving depth to Hulk's darker, intriguing side. The script handles the duality of Bruce Banner and Hulk with deftness, never overstepping its bounds while managing to maintain an ever-thrumming sense of high intensity and drama.

The Incredible Hulk serves its purpose as an enthralling action movie with fantastic special effects that captivate the audience. The interactions between Bruce Banner and Betty Ross, played convincingly by Liv Tyler, are heartwarming and provide relief to the otherwise intense narrative.

The film also boasts a plausible and compelling villain in the form of Emil Blonsky/The Abomination, portrayed by Tim Roth, who challenges Hulk on a physical and personal level. In conclusion, "The Incredible Hulk" is a compelling and enjoyable superhero film that is worth your time. While it might not be the most lauded Marvel enterprise, its pulsating action sequences complemented by a thought-provoking narrative about personal battles, make it a memorable experience. Credit must be given where it’s due and Norton's Hulk remains one of the standout performances in Marvel's early cinematic catalogue.

During World War I it had some strong links to the Western Fronts but this gradually diminished over time leaving it at times overshadowed by nearby Northcote and Maribyrnong. The town later rose against compulsory recruitment for the Australian Defence Force but the policy ended a few years after Australia entered World War II. The suburb grew rapidly during this period and began to lose some of its rural character. After WWII came through, more people joined the defence forces than left, which resulted in the city becoming more prosperous.[1] St Clair became home primarily to military personnel as Gourdum, Carshalton, Karratha and Duntroon merged with neighbouring towns before Cattai; Cavan-Monaro followed in 1967 due to military increases on station and also a new township coming to Beechworth called Greenhill. The city retained its status as a service community until 1970 when many soldiers were withdrawn. St Clair's population dropped from about 90 per cent pre war to 70 per cent post war then fell slightly again in 1990, following massive unemployment experienced by young residents in Melbourne. This trend was mirrored around the northern end of Goulburn Valley and along the railway line into Rockingham and Lismore where Goulburn has remained close to 10 thousand residents until the 2000 census. Some older families still look forward to a day when their children are too old or ill to work. There have also been cases of elderly and mentally troubled Stclair residents travelling down for work with family at stations along the way—a situation described as 'the shirking curse' by one older man from Wilsons Promontory that he found himself caught up in after being dismissed with other workers. In the early 21st Century the city remains somewhat detached although not so isolated now that most Goulburn Station offices close at 5pm each weekday.

The CNN-based methods have achieved impressive results in medical image
segmentation, but it failed to capture the long-range dependencies due to the
inherent locality of convolution operation. Transformer-based methods are
popular in vision tasks recently because of its capacity of long-range
dependencies and get a promising performance. However, it lacks in modeling
local context, although some works attempted to embed convolutional layer to
overcome this problem and achieved some improvement, but it makes the feature
inconsistent and fails to leverage the natural multi-scale features of
hierarchical transformer, which limit the performance of models. In this paper,
taking medical image segmentation as an example, we present MISSFormer, an
effective and powerful Medical Image Segmentation tranSFormer. MISSFormer is a
hierarchical encoder-decoder network and has two appealing designs: 1) A feed
forward network is redesigned with the proposed Enhanced Transformer Block,
which makes features aligned adaptively and enhances the long-range
dependencies and local context. 2) We proposed Enhanced Transformer Context
Bridge, a context bridge with the enhanced transformer block to model the
long-range dependencies and local context of multi-scale features generated by
our hierarchical transformer encoder. Driven by these two designs, the
MISSFormer shows strong capacity to capture more valuable dependencies and
context in medical image segmentation. The experiments on multi-organ and
cardiac segmentation tasks demonstrate the superiority, effectiveness and
robustness of our MISSFormer, the exprimental results of MISSFormer trained
from scratch even outperforms state-of-the-art methods pretrained on ImageNet,
and the core designs can be generalized to other visual segmentation tasks. The
code will be released in Github.

We present ObSuRF, a method which turns a single image of a scene into a 3D
model represented as a set of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), with each NeRF
corresponding to a different object. A single forward pass of an encoder
network outputs a set of latent vectors describing the objects in the scene.
These vectors are used independently to condition a NeRF decoder, defining the
geometry and appearance of each object. We make learning more computationally
efficient by deriving a novel loss, which allows training NeRFs on RGB-D inputs
without explicit ray marching. After confirming that the model performs equal
or better than state of the art on three 2D image segmentation benchmarks, we
apply it to two multi-object 3D datasets: A multiview version of CLEVR, and a
novel dataset in which scenes are populated by ShapeNet models. We find that
after training ObSuRF on RGB-D views of training scenes, it is capable of not
only recovering the 3D geometry of a scene depicted in a single input image,
but also to segment it into objects, despite receiving no supervision in that
regard.

To model recurrent interaction events in continuous time, an extension of the
stochastic block model is proposed where every individual belongs to a latent
group and interactions between two individuals follow a conditional
inhomogeneous Poisson process with intensity driven by the individuals' latent
groups. The model is shown to be identifiable and its estimation is based on a
semiparametric variational expectation-maximization algorithm. Two versions of
the method are developed, using either a nonparametric histogram approach (with
an adaptive choice of the partition size) or kernel intensity estimators. The
number of latent groups can be selected by an integrated classification
likelihood criterion. Finally, we demonstrate the performance of our procedure
on synthetic experiments, analyse two datasets to illustrate the utility of our
approach and comment on competing methods.

We study the applicability of a set of texture descriptors introduced in
recent work by the author to texture-based segmentation of images. The texture
descriptors under investigation result from applying graph indices from
quantitative graph theory to graphs encoding the local structure of images. The
underlying graphs arise from the computation of morphological amoebas as
structuring elements for adaptive morphology, either as weighted or unweighted
Dijkstra search trees or as edge-weighted pixel graphs within structuring
elements. In the present paper we focus on texture descriptors in which the
graph indices are entropy-based, and use them in a geodesic active contour
framework for image segmentation. Experiments on several synthetic and one
real-world image are shown to demonstrate texture segmentation by this
approach. Forthermore, we undertake an attempt to analyse selected
entropy-based texture descriptors with regard to what information about texture
they actually encode. Whereas this analysis uses some heuristic assumptions, it
indicates that the graph-based texture descriptors are related to fractal
dimension measures that have been proven useful in texture analysis.

Traditional NBA player evaluation metrics are based on scoring differential
or some pace-adjusted linear combination of box score statistics like points,
rebounds, assists, etc. These measures treat performances with the outcome of
the game still in question (e.g. tie score with five minutes left) in exactly
the same way as they treat performances with the outcome virtually decided
(e.g. when one team leads by 30 points with one minute left). Because they
ignore the context in which players perform, these measures can result in
misleading estimates of how players help their teams win. We instead use a win
probability framework for evaluating the impact NBA players have on their
teams' chances of winning. We propose a Bayesian linear regression model to
estimate an individual player's impact, after controlling for the other players
on the court. We introduce several posterior summaries to derive rank-orderings
of players within their team and across the league. This allows us to identify
highly paid players with low impact relative to their teammates, as well as
players whose high impact is not captured by existing metrics.

Learning is a complex cognitive process that depends not only on an
individual capability of knowledge absorption but it can be also influenced by
various group interactions and by the structure of an academic curriculum. We
have applied methods of statistical analyses and data mining (Principal
Component Analysis and Maximal Spanning Tree) for anonymized students' scores
at Faculty of Physics, Warsaw University of Technology. A slight negative
linear correlation exists between mean and variance of course grades, i.e.
courses with higher mean scores tend to possess a lower scores variance.
  There are courses playing a central role, e.g. their scores are highly
correlated to other scores and they are in the centre of corresponding Maximal
Spanning Trees. Other courses contribute significantly to students' score
variance as well to the first principal component and they are responsible for
differentiation of students' scores. Correlations of the first principal
component to courses' mean scores and scores variance suggest that this
component can be used for assigning ECTS points to a given course. The analyse
is independent from declared curricula of considered courses. The proposed
methodology is universal and can be applied for analysis of student's scores
and academic curriculum at any faculty.

The medical image is characterized by the inter-class indistinction, high
variability, and noise, where the recognition of pixels is challenging. Unlike
previous self-attention based methods that capture context information from one
level, we reformulate the self-attention mechanism from the view of the
high-order graph and propose a novel method, namely Hierarchical Attention
Network (HANet), to address the problem of medical image segmentation.
Concretely, an HA module embedded in the HANet captures context information
from neighbors of multiple levels, where these neighbors are extracted from the
high-order graph. In the high-order graph, there will be an edge between two
nodes only if the correlation between them is high enough, which naturally
reduces the noisy attention information caused by the inter-class
indistinction. The proposed HA module is robust to the variance of input and
can be flexibly inserted into the existing convolution neural networks. We
conduct experiments on three medical image segmentation tasks including optic
disc/cup segmentation, blood vessel segmentation, and lung segmentation.
Extensive results show our method is more effective and robust than the
existing state-of-the-art methods.

We investigate Referring Image Segmentation (RIS), which outputs a
segmentation map corresponding to the given natural language description. To
solve RIS efficiently, we need to understand each word's relationship with
other words, each region in the image to other regions, and cross-modal
alignment between linguistic and visual domains. We argue that one of the
limiting factors in the recent methods is that they do not handle these
interactions simultaneously. To this end, we propose a novel architecture
called JRNet, which uses a Joint Reasoning Module(JRM) to concurrently capture
the inter-modal and intra-modal interactions. The output of JRM is passed
through a novel Cross-Modal Multi-Level Fusion (CMMLF) module which further
refines the segmentation masks by exchanging contextual information across
visual hierarchy through linguistic features acting as a bridge. We present
thorough ablation studies and validate our approach's performance on four
benchmark datasets, showing considerable performance gains over the existing
state-of-the-art methods.

Myocardial contrast echocardiography (MCE) is an imaging technique that
assesses left ventricle function and myocardial perfusion for the detection of
coronary artery diseases. Automatic MCE perfusion quantification is challenging
and requires accurate segmentation of the myocardium from noisy and
time-varying images. Random forests (RF) have been successfully applied to many
medical image segmentation tasks. However, the pixel-wise RF classifier ignores
contextual relationships between label outputs of individual pixels. RF which
only utilizes local appearance features is also susceptible to data suffering
from large intensity variations. In this paper, we demonstrate how to overcome
the above limitations of classic RF by presenting a fully automatic
segmentation pipeline for myocardial segmentation in full-cycle 2D MCE data.
Specifically, a statistical shape model is used to provide shape prior
information that guide the RF segmentation in two ways. First, a novel shape
model (SM) feature is incorporated into the RF framework to generate a more
accurate RF probability map. Second, the shape model is fitted to the RF
probability map to refine and constrain the final segmentation to plausible
myocardial shapes. We further improve the performance by introducing a bounding
box detection algorithm as a preprocessing step in the segmentation pipeline.
Our approach on 2D image is further extended to 2D+t sequence which ensures
temporal consistency in the resultant sequence segmentations. When evaluated on
clinical MCE data, our proposed method achieves notable improvement in
segmentation accuracy and outperforms other state-of-the-art methods including
the classic RF and its variants, active shape model and image registration.

Despite the remarkable performance of deep learning methods on various tasks,
most cutting-edge models rely heavily on large-scale annotated training
examples, which are often unavailable for clinical and health care tasks. The
labeling costs for medical images are very high, especially in medical image
segmentation, which typically requires intensive pixel/voxel-wise labeling.
Therefore, the strong capability of learning and generalizing from limited
supervision, including a limited amount of annotations, sparse annotations, and
inaccurate annotations, is crucial for the successful application of deep
learning models in medical image segmentation. However, due to its intrinsic
difficulty, segmentation with limited supervision is challenging and specific
model design and/or learning strategies are needed. In this paper, we provide a
systematic and up-to-date review of the solutions above, with summaries and
comments about the methodologies. We also highlight several problems in this
field, discussed future directions observing further investigations.

The idea of stable, localized bundles of energy has strong appeal as a model
for particles. In the 1950s John Wheeler envisioned such bundles as smooth
configurations of electromagnetic energy that he called {\em geons}, but none
were found. Instead, particle-like solutions were found in the late 1960s with
the addition of a scalar field, and these were given the name {\em boson
stars}. Since then, boson stars find use in a wide variety of models as sources
of dark matter, as black hole mimickers, in simple models of binary systems,
and as a tool in finding black holes in higher dimensions with only a single
killing vector. We discuss important varieties of boson stars, their dynamic
properties, and some of their uses, concentrating on recent efforts.

Image segmentation methods are usually trained with pixel-level annotations,
which require significant human effort to collect. The most common solution to
address this constraint is to implement weakly-supervised pipelines trained
with lower forms of supervision, such as bounding boxes or scribbles. Another
option are semi-supervised methods, which leverage a large amount of unlabeled
data and a limited number of strongly-labeled samples. In this second setup,
samples to be strongly-annotated can be selected randomly or with an active
learning mechanism that chooses the ones that will maximize the model
performance. In this work, we propose a sample selection approach to decide
which samples to annotate for semi-supervised instance segmentation. Our method
consists in first predicting pseudo-masks for the unlabeled pool of samples,
together with a score predicting the quality of the mask. This score is an
estimate of the Intersection Over Union (IoU) of the segment with the ground
truth mask. We study which samples are better to annotate given the quality
score, and show how our approach outperforms a random selection, leading to
improved performance for semi-supervised instance segmentation with low
annotation budgets.

Grebinski and Kucherov (1998) and Alon et al. (2004-2005) study the problem
of learning a hidden graph for some especial cases, such as hamiltonian cycle,
cliques, stars, and matchings. This problem is motivated by problems in
chemical reactions, molecular biology and genome sequencing.
  In this paper, we present a generalization of this problem. Precisely, we
consider a graph G and a subgraph H of G and we assume that G contains exactly
one defective subgraph isomorphic to H. The goal is to find the defective
subgraph by testing whether an induced subgraph contains an edge of the
defective subgraph, with the minimum number of tests. We present an upper bound
for the number of tests to find the defective subgraph by using the symmetric
and high probability variation of Lov\'asz Local Lemma.

Inspired by the combination of feedforward and iterative computations in the
virtual cortex, and taking advantage of the ability of denoising autoencoders
to estimate the score of a joint distribution, we propose a novel approach to
iterative inference for capturing and exploiting the complex joint distribution
of output variables conditioned on some input variables. This approach is
applied to image pixel-wise segmentation, with the estimated conditional score
used to perform gradient ascent towards a mode of the estimated conditional
distribution. This extends previous work on score estimation by denoising
autoencoders to the case of a conditional distribution, with a novel use of a
corrupted feedforward predictor replacing Gaussian corruption. An advantage of
this approach over more classical ways to perform iterative inference for
structured outputs, like conditional random fields (CRFs), is that it is not
any more necessary to define an explicit energy function linking the output
variables. To keep computations tractable, such energy function
parametrizations are typically fairly constrained, involving only a few
neighbors of each of the output variables in each clique. We experimentally
find that the proposed iterative inference from conditional score estimation by
conditional denoising autoencoders performs better than comparable models based
on CRFs or those not using any explicit modeling of the conditional joint
distribution of outputs.

A stable generalized complex structure is one that is generically symplectic
but degenerates along a real codimension two submanifold, where it defines a
generalized Calabi-Yau structure. We introduce a Lie algebroid which allows us
to view such structures as symplectic forms. This allows us to construct new
examples of stable structures, and also to define period maps for their
deformations in which the background three-form flux is either fixed or not,
proving the unobstructedness of both deformation problems. We then use the same
tools to establish local normal forms for the degeneracy locus and for
Lagrangian branes. Applying our normal forms to the four-dimensional case, we
prove that any compact stable generalized complex 4-manifold has a symplectic
completion, in the sense that it can be modified near its degeneracy locus to
produce a compact symplectic 4-manifold.

Automatic histopathology image segmentation is crucial to disease analysis.
Limited available labeled data hinders the generalizability of trained models
under the fully supervised setting. Semi-supervised learning (SSL) based on
generative methods has been proven to be effective in utilizing diverse image
characteristics. However, it has not been well explored what kinds of generated
images would be more useful for model training and how to use such images. In
this paper, we propose a new data guided generative method for histopathology
image segmentation by leveraging the unlabeled data distributions. First, we
design an image generation module. Image content and style are disentangled and
embedded in a clustering-friendly space to utilize their distributions. New
images are synthesized by sampling and cross-combining contents and styles.
Second, we devise an effective data selection policy for judiciously sampling
the generated images: (1) to make the generated training set better cover the
dataset, the clusters that are underrepresented in the original training set
are covered more; (2) to make the training process more effective, we identify
and oversample the images of "hard cases" in the data for which annotated
training data may be scarce. Our method is evaluated on glands and nuclei
datasets. We show that under both the inductive and transductive settings, our
SSL method consistently boosts the performance of common segmentation models
and attains state-of-the-art results.

State-of-the-art semantic image segmentation methods are mostly based on
training deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). In this work, we proffer to
improve semantic segmentation with the use of contextual information. In
particular, we explore `patch-patch' context and `patch-background' context in
deep CNNs. We formulate deep structured models by combining CNNs and
Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) for learning the patch-patch context between
image regions. Specifically, we formulate CNN-based pairwise potential
functions to capture semantic correlations between neighboring patches.
Efficient piecewise training of the proposed deep structured model is then
applied in order to avoid repeated expensive CRF inference during the course of
back propagation. For capturing the patch-background context, we show that a
network design with traditional multi-scale image inputs and sliding pyramid
pooling is very effective for improving performance. We perform comprehensive
evaluation of the proposed method. We achieve new state-of-the-art performance
on a number of challenging semantic segmentation datasets including $NYUDv2$,
$PASCAL$-$VOC2012$, $Cityscapes$, $PASCAL$-$Context$, $SUN$-$RGBD$,
$SIFT$-$flow$, and $KITTI$ datasets. Particularly, we report an
intersection-over-union score of $77.8$ on the $PASCAL$-$VOC2012$ dataset.

We present a new test when there is a nuisance parameter under the
alternative hypothesis. The test exploits the p-value occupation time [PVOT],
the measure of the nuisance parameter subset on which a p-value test based on a
a test statistic rejects the null hypothesis. Key contributions are: (i) An
asymptotic critical value upper bound for our test is the significance level
{\alpha}, making inference easy. (ii) We only require the test statistic to
have a known or bootstrappable limit distribution, hence we do not require
root(n)-Gaussian asymptotics, allowing for weak or non-identification, boundary
values, heavy tails, infill asymptotics, and so on. (iii) A test based on the
sup-p-value may be conservative and in some cases have trivial power, while the
PVOT naturally controls for this by smoothing over the nuisance parameter
space. Finally, (iv) the PVOT uniquely allows for bootstrap inference in the
presence of nuisance parameters when some estimated parameters may not be
identified.

We give a graph-sum algorithm that expresses any genus-$g$ Gromov-Witten
invariant of the symmetric product orbifold
$\mathrm{Sym}^d\mathbb{P}^r:=[(\mathbb{P}^r)^d/S_d]$ in terms of "Hurwitz-Hodge
integrals" -- integrals over (compactified) Hurwitz spaces. We apply the
algorithm to prove a partial mirror theorem for $\mathrm{Sym}^d\mathbb{P}^r$ in
genus zero. The theorem states that a generating function of Gromov-Witten
invariants of $\mathrm{Sym}^d\mathbb{P}^r$ is equal to an explicit power series
$I_{\mathrm{Sym}^d\mathbb{P}^r},$ conditional upon a conjectural combinatorial
identity. This is a first step towards proving Ruan's Crepant Resolution
Conjecture for the resolution $\mathrm{Hilb}^{(d)}(\mathbb{P}^2)$ of the coarse
moduli space of $\mathrm{Sym}^d\mathbb{P}^2.$

We propose a novel locally adaptive learning estimator for enhancing the
inter- and intra- discriminative capabilities of Deep Neural Networks, which
can be used as improved loss layer for semantic image segmentation tasks. Most
loss layers compute pixel-wise cost between feature maps and ground truths,
ignoring spatial layouts and interactions between neighboring pixels with same
object category, and thus networks cannot be effectively sensitive to
intra-class connections. Stride by stride, our method firstly conducts adaptive
pooling filter operating over predicted feature maps, aiming to merge predicted
distributions over a small group of neighboring pixels with same category, and
then it computes cost between the merged distribution vector and their category
label. Such design can make groups of neighboring predictions from same
category involved into estimations on predicting correctness with respect to
their category, and hence train networks to be more sensitive to regional
connections between adjacent pixels based on their categories. In the
experiments on Pascal VOC 2012 segmentation datasets, the consistently improved
results show that our proposed approach achieves better segmentation masks
against previous counterparts.

Contemporary deep learning based medical image segmentation algorithms
require hours of annotation labor by domain experts. These data hungry deep
models perform sub-optimally in the presence of limited amount of labeled data.
In this paper, we present a data efficient learning framework using the recent
concept of Generative Adversarial Networks; this allows a deep neural network
to perform significantly better than its fully supervised counterpart in low
annotation regime. The proposed method is an extension of our previous work
with the addition of a new unsupervised adversarial loss and a structured
prediction based architecture. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the
first demonstration of an adversarial framework based structured prediction
model for medical image segmentation. Though generic, we apply our method for
segmentation of blood vessels in retinal fundus images. We experiment with
extreme low annotation budget (0.8 - 1.6% of contemporary annotation size). On
DRIVE and STARE datasets, the proposed method outperforms our previous method
and other fully supervised benchmark models by significant margins especially
with very low number of annotated examples. In addition, our systematic
ablation studies suggest some key recipes for successfully training GAN based
semi-supervised algorithms with an encoder-decoder style network architecture.

In this paper, we review and substantially develop the recently proposed
"Microscopic Response Method", which has been devised to compute transport
coefficients and especially associated temperature dependence in complex
materials. The conductivity and Hall mobility of amorphous semiconductors and
semiconducting polymers are systematically derived, and shown to be more
practical than the Kubo formalism. The effect of a quantized lattice (phonons)
on transport coefficients is fully included and then integrated out, providing
the primary temperature dependence for the transport coefficients. For
higher-order processes, using a diagrammatic expansion, one can consistently
include all important contributions to a given order and directly write out the
expressions of transport coefficients for various processes.

In this survey we give an overview of recent developments on the Quantitative
Subspace Theorem. In particular, we discuss a new upper bound for the number of
subspaces containing the "large" solutions, obtained jointly with Roberto
Ferretti, and sketch the proof of the latter. Further, we prove a new gap
principle to handle the "small" solutions in the system of inequalities
considered in the Subspace Theorem. Finally, we go into the refinement of the
Subspace Theorem by Faltings and Wuestholz, which states that the system of
inequalities considered has only finitely many solutions outside some
effectively determinable proper linear subspace of the ambient solution space.
Estimating the number of these solutions is still an open problem. We give some
motivation that this problem is very hard.

Image segmentation is the problem of partitioning an image into different
subsets, where each subset may have a different characterization in terms of
color, intensity, texture, and/or other features. Segmentation is a fundamental
component of image processing, and plays a significant role in computer vision,
object recognition, and object tracking. Active Contour Models (ACMs)
constitute a powerful energy-based minimization framework for image
segmentation, which relies on the concept of contour evolution. Starting from
an initial guess, the contour is evolved with the aim of approximating better
and better the actual object boundary. Handling complex images in an efficient,
effective, and robust way is a real challenge, especially in the presence of
intensity inhomogeneity, overlap between the foreground/background intensity
distributions, objects characterized by many different intensities, and/or
additive noise. In this thesis, to deal with these challenges, we propose a
number of image segmentation models relying on variational level set methods
and specific kinds of neural networks, to handle complex images in both
supervised and unsupervised ways. Experimental results demonstrate the high
accuracy of the segmentation results, obtained by the proposed models on
various benchmark synthetic and real images compared with state-of-the-art
active contour models.

Spleen volume estimation using automated image segmentation technique may be
used to detect splenomegaly (abnormally enlarged spleen) on Magnetic Resonance
Imaging (MRI) scans. In recent years, Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNN)
segmentation methods have demonstrated advantages for abdominal organ
segmentation. However, variations in both size and shape of the spleen on MRI
images may result in large false positive and false negative labeling when
deploying DCNN based methods. In this paper, we propose the Splenomegaly
Segmentation Network (SSNet) to address spatial variations when segmenting
extraordinarily large spleens. SSNet was designed based on the framework of
image-to-image conditional generative adversarial networks (cGAN).
Specifically, the Global Convolutional Network (GCN) was used as the generator
to reduce false negatives, while the Markovian discriminator (PatchGAN) was
used to alleviate false positives. A cohort of clinically acquired 3D MRI scans
(both T1 weighted and T2 weighted) from patients with splenomegaly were used to
train and test the networks. The experimental results demonstrated that a mean
Dice coefficient of 0.9260 and a median Dice coefficient of 0.9262 using SSNet
on independently tested MRI volumes of patients with splenomegaly.

Image Segmentation has been an active field of research as it has a wide
range of applications, ranging from automated disease detection to self-driving
cars. In recent years, various research papers proposed different loss
functions used in case of biased data, sparse segmentation, and unbalanced
dataset. In this paper, we introduce SemSegLoss, a python package consisting of
some of the well-known loss functions widely used for image segmentation. It is
developed with the intent to help researchers in the development of novel loss
functions and perform an extensive set of experiments on model architectures
for various applications. The ease-of-use and flexibility of the presented
package have allowed reducing the development time and increased evaluation
strategies of machine learning models for semantic segmentation. Furthermore,
different applications that use image segmentation can use SemSegLoss because
of the generality of its functions. This wide range of applications will lead
to the development and growth of AI across all industries.

We apply the methods of transformation optics to theoretical descriptions of
spacetimes that support closed null geodesic curves. The metric used is based
on frame dragging spacetimes, such as the van Stockum dust or the Kerr black
hole. Through transformation optics, this metric is analogous to a material
that in theory should allow for communication between past and future.
Presented herein is a derivation and description of the spacetime and the
resulting permeability, permittivity, and magneto-electric couplings that a
material would need in order for light in the material to follow closed null
geodesics. We also address the paradoxical implications of such a material, and
demonstrate why such a material would not actually result in a violation of
causality. A full derivation of the Plebanski equations is also included.

Recent progress in biomedical image segmentation based on deep convolutional
neural networks (CNNs) has drawn much attention. However, its vulnerability
towards adversarial samples cannot be overlooked. This paper is the first one
that discovers that all the CNN-based state-of-the-art biomedical image
segmentation models are sensitive to adversarial perturbations. This limits the
deployment of these methods in safety-critical biomedical fields. In this
paper, we discover that global spatial dependencies and global contextual
information in a biomedical image can be exploited to defend against
adversarial attacks. To this end, non-local context encoder (NLCE) is proposed
to model short- and long range spatial dependencies and encode global contexts
for strengthening feature activations by channel-wise attention. The NLCE
modules enhance the robustness and accuracy of the non-local context encoding
network (NLCEN), which learns robust enhanced pyramid feature representations
with NLCE modules, and then integrates the information across different levels.
Experiments on both lung and skin lesion segmentation datasets have
demonstrated that NLCEN outperforms any other state-of-the-art biomedical image
segmentation methods against adversarial attacks. In addition, NLCE modules can
be applied to improve the robustness of other CNN-based biomedical image
segmentation methods.

Image segmentation is a vital part of image processing. Segmentation has its
application widespread in the field of medical images in order to diagnose
curious diseases. The same medical images can be segmented manually. But the
accuracy of image segmentation using the segmentation algorithms is more when
compared with the manual segmentation. In the field of medical diagnosis an
extensive diversity of imaging techniques is presently available, such as
radiography, computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
Medical image segmentation is an essential step for most consequent image
analysis tasks. Although the original FCM algorithm yields good results for
segmenting noise free images, it fails to segment images corrupted by noise,
outliers and other imaging artifact. This paper presents an image segmentation
approach using Modified Fuzzy C-Means (FCM) algorithm and Fuzzy Possibilistic
c-means algorithm (FPCM). This approach is a generalized version of standard
Fuzzy CMeans Clustering (FCM) algorithm. The limitation of the conventional FCM
technique is eliminated in modifying the standard technique. The Modified FCM
